To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
melatonin receptor sub-types Mel1a and 1c are expressed on the lateral membrane of surface corneal cells of the Xenopus laeves.
melatonin receptors are expressed in Xenopus surface CE in a dynamic manner that is consistent with the concept that melatonine may regulate circadian activity of the surface CE.
all three melatonin receptor isoforms are expressed in the surface epithelial cells of the cornea, but are differentially localized to specific subcellular domains of the cell.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of melatonin in the circadian control of the surface epithelial barrier in the Xenopus cornea, and we are particularly interested in the role of mel1a receptors in this process.
the circadian regulation of the surface corneal cell barrier, which is the first line of defense in the eye against microbial pathogens and toxic substances in the environment.

the role of the circadian clock and melatonin signaling in the surface corneal cell layer of Xenopus laevisthat regulates the permeability of the cornea and its transparency, and the role of the clock in the regulation of corneal epithelial cell differentiation and wound healing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the surface CE is an important site for melatonin receptor-mediated circadian regulation, and that melatonin signaling is likely to be an important regulator of corneal epithelial barrier function and/or permeability.

melatonin signaling in the corneal surface epithelium is dynamic and circadian regulated, and that the melatonin receptors are located in close proximity to tight junctions, suggesting the possibility that melatonin signaling is involved in the formation or breakdown of tight junctions, which would influence corneal epithelial barrier function and the permeability of the corneal stroma.
the melatonin receptors, Mel1a and possibly Mel1c, are expressed in the surface corneal cells of the Xenopus laeavis cornea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown the expression and sub-cellular localization of melatonin receptors in a vertebrate corneal epithelial tissue, and we have also shown that the melatonin receptors are located in a position that is in close association with the tight junctions.
we have identified the presence of melatonin receptors on the corneal surface and that their localization changes with time.

we have shown for the first time the presence of Mel1a receptors in the lateral membrane of the surface corneal cells of Xenopus, and that these receptors are located in close proximity to ZO-1 proteins that form the tight junction barrier.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Mel1c melatonin receptor subtype is expressed in the Xenopus corneal epithelial surface epithelium and that its localization and distribution is dynamic throughout the circadian cycle.
the surface epithelum of the Xenopus laeis cornea expresses melatonin receptor sub-type 1a, 1b and 1c, with a diurnal rhythm of lateral plasma membrane localization.
the Mel1b and Mel1c subtypes are expressed on the surface CE of the Xenopus laevi, and the expression and localization of the receptors oscillates during the day.
